summary: The lecture explains three methods of computing GDP—Production (Value-Added), Income, and Expenditure—using a cricket bat economy example. It details the transition from GDP at Market Price to GNP and National Income by adjusting for Net Factor Income from Abroad, Depreciation, and Net Indirect Taxes. It distinguishes Nominal GDP (current prices) from Real GDP (base year 2011-12 prices) to measure true economic growth. Finally, it highlights the difference between production and product taxes and the treatment of inventory and imputed rent.
points: Three GDP calculation methods: Production (Value-Added), Income, Expenditure; all yield same GDP value.
Value Added Method: GVA = Value of Output – Intermediate Consumption; avoids double counting of intermediate goods.
Expenditure Method: GDP = C + I + G + (X – M); includes inventory changes as investment.
Income Method: GDP = Wages (cash/kind) + Rent (imputed for self-owned) + Interest + Profit; includes imputed rent.
GDPMP includes Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) and Net Indirect Taxes (Production + Product taxes).
GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA); GDP is territorial, GNP is residential concept.
National Income (NNPFC) = GNPMP – Depreciation – Net Indirect Taxes.
Nominal GDP uses current prices; Real GDP uses base year (2011-12) prices to measure volume changes.
Economic Growth = Increase in Real GDP; Nominal GDP can mislead due to price changes.
Production taxes (stamp duty) are volume-independent; Product taxes (GST) vary with output volume.
